meta.title: Who really said "The ladder of success is never crowded at the top"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon Hill's 1970 book does print the line — but it was already in print, unsigned, in 1963, and it is not in Think and Grow Rich.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The ladder of success is never crowded at the top'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is real in a Hill book — the 1970 one he co-wrote. It appeared unattributed seven years earlier, and the coiner is unknown.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Hill’s name is genuinely on the sentence: it is printed on p. 247 of Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion (Fawcett Crest, 1970), the book he shares with co-author E. Harold Keown. But the same line was already circulating unsigned — word for word in a 1963 dental journal and a 1968 student paper, in garbled form in a 1965 classified ad — so the earliest documented printings carry no author, and nothing ties the wording to anything Hill published earlier. Barry Popik, who compiled that record, adds that Hill may well have used the saying before then in lectures or articles.

source.excerpt: The ladder of success is never crowded at the top.
trail: 1963 — the sentence appears in the West Virginia Dental Journal (vols. 36–37, p. 35), set in capitals with no author attached, the earliest printing in Barry Popik’s record ↗.

1965 and 1968 — a classified ad in The News of Van Nuys, California and a fraternity column in the Tri-State Triangle both run the line as an anonymous slogan, still with no writer’s name, in the same citation list ↗.

1970 — Napoleon Hill and E. Harold Keown print it on p. 247 of Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion, the year Hill died; the Fawcett Crest edition is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗. This is the earliest appearance under Hill’s name that Popik documents.
Today — the credit has hardened into ‘Napoleon Hill’, though AZQuotes’s own citation points to a 2016 compilation ↗ and Wikiquote’s Hill page carries the line in no section at all ↗.
source.excerptNote: Popik records the line at p. 247 as a free-standing maxim, with no surrounding argument quoted — the same way it ran in 1963, where the West Virginia Dental Journal printed it in capitals with no author attached. (Google Books dates that volume 1962; Popik corrects the reading to 1963.)

source.rightsNote: Nothing here is safely public domain. The earliest documented printing, in 1963, carries no author, so no rights holder can be identified for the wording itself — and the earliest printing under Hill’s name, Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion (1970), is a modern in-copyright book. Treat the sentence as a short maxim of unknown ownership, not as free-and-clear text; only the nineteenth-century ancestor proverb, ‘there’s always room at the top’, is genuinely out of copyright, and that is different wording.

author.name: Napoleon Hill
author.heading: The man the line lands on
author.bio: Napoleon Hill built the template for American success writing with Think and Grow Rich (1937), still among the best-selling self-help books ever published. The book rests on a claimed commission from Andrew Carnegie to codify the habits of the rich — a collaboration for which historians have never found supporting evidence, along with much of the rest of Hill’s self-told biography. He kept publishing to the end of his life in 1970, and the foundation and estate that survive him have issued compilations under his name ever since, which is how lines he merely quoted end up filed as things he said.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the usual credit
misattribution.intro: Hill really did print this sentence, which makes the quote unusual: the name is half-right and everything attached to it is wrong.

items.why: Quote pages, posters and social posts routinely file the line under Hill’s famous 1937 bestseller. It is not there — a searchable full text of the book contains no occurrence of ‘crowded at the top’, and its three uses of ‘ladder’ are unrelated (‘half way up the ladder’, ‘the ladder of creative effort’) — and the earliest printing anyone has documented is 1963, twenty-six years after the book appeared, per Barry Popik’s chronology ↗.

Before Hill’s 1970 book, the line runs three times with no author attached: a 1963 West Virginia Dental Journal line set in capitals, a 1965 Van Nuys classified ad and a 1968 Tri-State College student column, all listed by Popik ↗. Popik does not rule Hill out — he thinks it probable Hill was using the saying earlier in lectures or articles — but no such use has ever been documented, and Hill shared that 1970 title with E. Harold Keown, so even the book page cannot be pinned on Hill alone.

Where the big aggregators cite anything at all, it is a modern compilation rather than a book Hill saw into print: AZQuotes sources the line to Napoleon Hill and Judith Williamson, Do It Now! (2016), p. 52 ↗ — assembled 46 years after Hill died.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: a mid-century motto in print unsigned by 1963, whose coiner is undocumented. It acquired a famous name seven years later when Hill and Keown put it in Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion — and Barry Popik, who compiled the citation record ↗, allows that Hill himself may have been circulating it earlier in lectures or articles, though no such use is documented.

context.heading: The staircase before the ladder
lead: The thought is far older than Hill. Nineteenth-century America already had the proverb ‘there’s always room at the top’, usually told as a Daniel Webster anecdote: warned off the law because the profession was overcrowded, the young Webster is supposed to have replied that there was room enough at the top. The Oxford English Dictionary’s first citation for the phrase is an 1866 Maine newspaper retelling exactly that story, collected with the earlier versions by Barry Popik ↗.

By 1871 a Louisiana paper was printing verse built on the same contrast — jammed at the bottom, empty at the top — which is the whole argument of the modern line already fully formed. The twentieth century swapped Webster’s staircase for a ladder, dressed it as an office motto, and eventually pinned a famous motivational name on it.
context.detailsSummary: Even the Webster version is hearsay
detailsBody: The earliest retellings do not claim to quote Webster directly. Edward Everett Hale’s 1852 sermon footnotes the remark as ‘Mr. Webster’s, as I have heard it quoted, as if used by him in conversation’, and an 1855 essay collection introduces it with ‘Mr. Webster is said to have stated’. Both give the words as ‘there is room higher up’, not the familiar ‘room at the top’ — see Popik’s transcriptions ↗. The proverb this quote descends from is itself an attribution problem.
context.pull: Remember the low grounds are crowded, / But there’s always room at the top. — anonymous newspaper verse, 1871

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest documented printing of "The ladder of success is never crowded at the top" is the West Virginia Dental Journal, vols. 36-37 (1963), p. 35, set in capitals with no author attached (Google Books dates the volume 1962; Popik corrects to 1963); later unattributed printings appear in a Van Nuys classified ad (8 June 1965) and the Tri-State Triangle (7 Nov 1968); Napoleon Hill and E. Harold Keown print it on p. 247 of Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion (Fawcett Crest, 1970); an Omaha World-Herald ad of 20 Sept 1971 uses the variant "is not crowded at the top"; 2004 and 2011 quote books credit Napoleon Hill.

The older proverb behind the line is "there's always room at the top"; the OED's first citation is the Bangor (Maine) Daily Whig & Courier, 27 Feb 1866, retelling the Daniel Webster anecdote; earlier 1852 and 1855 retellings give it as "room higher up" and describe it only as something Webster was said to have remarked in conversation; an 1871 Louisiana newspaper poem reads "Remember the low grounds are crowded, / But there's always room at the top."
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion by Napoleon Hill (1883-1970), associated name E. Harold Keown, published New York: Fawcett Crest, 1970.

Napoleon Hill lived 26 October 1883 to 8 November 1970, was an American self-help author best known for Think and Grow Rich (1937), co-wrote Succeed and Grow Rich Through Persuasion (1970) with E. Harold Keown, and his claimed collaboration with Andrew Carnegie is unsupported by evidence.
Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill page contains no entry with the words "ladder" or "crowded" in any section; the phrase "The ladder of success is never crowded at the top" does not appear on the page.

AZQuotes attributes "The ladder of success is never crowded at the top" to Napoleon Hill and gives as its citation: Napoleon Hill, Judith Williamson (2016), "Do It Now!", p. 52, Jaico Publishing House.
